summary:
Raphael Kalandadze frames post-launch operations as 'the missing layer' that most agent talks ignore—shipping is when the real work begins. Building an agent product is now the easy part; maintaining health across thousands of live conversations is the hard part. Agents differ from classical software because they are non-deterministic, have endless coverage, and cannot be fully pre-tested. Failures are often hidden: agents struggle mid-task, recover via luck or workarounds, and technically complete while failing the user (e.g., building a trip itinerary but miscalculating prices). Normal safety nets—unit tests, regex, rule-based checks, simulated conversations—only cover one slice. The source of truth is logs, and agents are better than humans at exploring them, but operating an agent is itself an agent problem requiring deep reasoning to distinguish bugs from noise and symptoms from root causes.

Kalandadze describes multiple operating agents working together as a 'meta harness.' A log monitoring agent with codebase access diagnoses problems and sends PRs every 15 minutes to an hour. A separate review agent with fresh context criticizes each PR, requests changes, or closes it, filtering bad fixes before humans. A session analyzer agent scores every conversation, detects high-level patterns, and produces a health dashboard with success rates, sentiment analysis, tool-call analytics, and AI-generated insights connecting dots across hundreds or thousands of sessions. A computer use agent opens a browser, logs in, and simulates the customer perspective to catch UI problems that logs and code cannot reveal—a custom DOM-aware skill makes this faster than general tools. All agents need access to trajectories, metrics, database, and UI to understand real problems. The PR and review agents together send ten times more PRs daily than the three-person human team. Humans remain at merge boundaries. Kalandadze's closing thesis: shipping is the easiest part today; teams must close the loop first, then optionally remove the human bottleneck later. The system itself—watching, understanding, and improving—is what differentiates a production agent.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Missing Layer After Launch
sections.summary: Kalandadze introduces the core thesis: most agent talks end at shipping, but shipping is when real work begins. The 'missing layer' is post-launch operations—monitoring, understanding health, and finding unknown holes across thousands of real conversations.

sections.title: Why Agent Operations Is Hard
sections.summary: Agents are non-deterministic with endless coverage. Normal safety nets (unit tests, regex, simulations) only cover a slice. Customers always behave differently. You lose the feel for your own system. Hidden failures include luck-based recovery and technical success that fails the user (e.g., trip itinerary with miscalculated prices).

sections.title: Operating Agents Is an Agent Problem
sections.summary: Logs are the source of truth and agents are best at exploring them, but diagnosing problems requires deep reasoning to distinguish bugs from noise and symptoms from root causes. The end-to-end flow: traces/trajectories feed a diagnostic agent with codebase access that sends PRs, then a separate review agent with fresh context criticizes and filters PRs before humans.

sections.title: Fast Loop: Log Monitoring Agent
sections.summary: The fast loop runs every 15 minutes to an hour, diagnosing problems, checking if users are stuck, sending PRs or Slack alerts. PR artifacts include descriptions, metadata, mermaid/ASCII diagrams, and HTML artifacts. The review agent requests changes or closes PRs. PR and review agents produce 10x more PRs daily than the three-person team. Humans stay at merge boundaries for now.

sections.title: High-Level Health Loop: Session Analyzer
sections.summary: The log monitoring agent handles local fixes but lacks high-level system understanding. A session analyzer agent scores every conversation, detects patterns, and produces a health dashboard with success rates, sentiment analysis, tool-call analytics, AI insights connecting dots, and per-session detailed analysis. Kalandadze built it in-house rather than using third-party tools because he knows what he is looking for. It runs weekly or a few times per week, covering hundreds or thousands of real conversations.

sections.title: Computer Use Agent: User Perspective
sections.summary: Log-based and code-based agents lack the user perspective. A computer use agent opens a browser, logs in, and simulates the customer to catch UI problems that logs cannot reveal. A custom DOM-aware skill makes this faster than general tools like Codex, but it is slow and token-intensive. When it detects problems, it should be able to analyze trajectories and check the database to understand what happened.

sections.title: Meta Harness and Closing the Loop
sections.summary: Kalandadze calls the whole connected system a 'meta harness'—agents that watch, understand, and improve themselves. The model alone is not enough; you need to build the system around it. All agents need access to trajectories, metrics, database, and UI. His closing thesis: shipping is the easiest part today; teams must close the loop first, then remove the human bottleneck. The internal system that detects problems and gives visibility into what is happening is what differentiates a production agent.
